Note that when your internship is over, you still need to get registered for the IE300 or IE400 courses in the Fall semester (or summer school if you are planning to).

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: Students who will do a SP this summer should carefully read the information below about “When to apply” and “How to apply” for the SGK insurance.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: When to apply for the SGK insurance

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: The ideal moment to apply for the insurance using the OCW system is 2-3 weeks before the beginning of your internship. To make the procedure work efficiently, let us follow these ground rules:

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 1. SGK insurance requests are processed by Rektörlük. As an internship committee our role is to make a pre-check the required info. and then deliver the requests to Rektörlük .

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 2. On the Monday morning of each week, the insurance applications of students beginning their internships within two weeks will be sent to Rektörlük. For example, the list sent on June 30, Monday covers the students with SP beginning dates between July 1 - July 11.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 2. For your SGK document to be issued smoothly and on time, you should leave a safety margin of 1 whole week (Monday to Friday) between your application and the beginning of your SP. For example, if your internship begins in the week of July 14-18, then the ideal moment to apply for the insurance is within the week June 30- July 4, so that your application is sent to Rektörlük on Monday July 7 and your document is issued on time.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 3. Please do not apply for the insurance too early (for instance, don’t apply 2 months before!). This is for two reasons:

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: Even if you apply early, Rektörlük does not process insurance applications that start in more than two weeks.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: There may often be changes in the SP plans of students, such as modifications in the SP beginning dates, cancellation of the SPs, etc. If you have already sent an application, this causes extra work for everyone.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 4. Please do not apply for the insurance too late, neither (for instance, don’t apply 5 days before your internship starts!) This is very likely to lead to delays in the preparation of your SGK document and causes extra work for everyone. Remember that the ideal time to apply is 2-3 weeks before the beginning of your SP. Please see also Rule 2 above to see when your application will be processed.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: How to apply for the SGK insurance

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 1. First, make sure that you already read the section “When to apply for the SGK insurance” above.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 2. To apply for the insurance, first login to https://ocw.metu.edu.tr/ with your usual student account. You should normally be already registered the IE 300/400 course, which you should be able to see under “My courses”. If you fail to see IE 300/400, please send an email to the SP committee (“ ie-staj at metu edu tr” ).

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 3. Click on IE 300/400 and you will see a list named “Required Information” in the course menu.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 4. Click on “SGK Insurance Application”, which takes you to a questionnaire where you must enter your identity and company information. Do not forget to click on “Submit Questionnaire” when you finish.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 5. Upload your "Declaration Form for students with/without family health insurance" form to the OCW system. The declaration form can be found at this link .

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 6. If you have successfully completed all these steps, then your application is done. You will not receive any notification or confirmation when your application is sent to Rektörlük , and you will still be able to view your application on the OCW system. This is normal since we use the “questionnaire” structure to collect your data and answers remain accessible.

title: General Information |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: 7. Your SGK insurance document will be available on e-devlet typically 2-3 workdays before the beginning of your SP. You can access your document on e-devlet by following these steps:

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: How can I arrange a summer practice organization?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: There are two alternatives; either you apply to organizations personally or wait for the summer practice opportunities announced by the department. The second option is more risky and the capacity is usually very limited. Certain firms require the department to determine the candidates for summer practice. In that case, an announcement is made and the students are required to send their transcripts, resumes and fill out the Preference Form available under >Forms. If the student is assigned through the department, it is mandatory that the summer practice is conducted at that company.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: Which departments of the organization should I visit during my summer practice?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: It is preferable for you to take an all-around trip in an organization. However, do not forget that you can still gather many observations through effective communications. You inquire about the overall operations in your practice organization although you are stationed at a particular department.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: What kind of topics will I be studying during the practice term?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: Industrial engineering has a broad application area. Its main field of interest is systems run by people for the needs of others, in general. Summer practice is your first lengthy period of observing and inquiring about systems in operation. Try as much as you can, to relate things you have covered in your courses to what you experience during your practice term. Learn about the many possible ways of getting various organizational and technical functions performed. Identify the systems behind all those activities. Use your "Summer Practice Manual" to guide you through this effort.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: What sort of branches or divisions in a bank are suitable for an IE 400 practice organization?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: As in many organizations banks have numerous activities in providing services to their customers. You should be more interested in the systems (for example organizational, information related, procedural, managerial) aspects in this service provision. In IE 400 Summer Practice you are required to observe and analyze a purposeful system in real life. Divisions or branches in a bank are suitable in that regard so much as they consist of integrated operation of people, financial resources, processes and information with some performance expectation, and they have ongoing decision making (for example, planning or evaluation) or development (for example, new services) as their required function.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: What constitutes a "sufficient" IE problem definition in IE 400 reports?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: This is described in Appendix A of your IE 400 Summer Practice Manual. You are required to supply your own description of the components of a problem formulation and justify your points. You should be specific to your practice organization. Problem identification should be the result of some methodical analysis carried out in the system the problem is associated with. Alternative courses of action and constraining factors should be supported by problem specific facts.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: How should a student answer questions in manufacturing oriented areas if the practice is done in a service organization?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: The critical issue is to see the analogies. If not exactly the same, you can identify areas of similar nature in a service organization. A budget allocation might substitute a production plan, preclassified records may stand as inventory, timetables for professionals can be counted as their schedules, from flow may replace material flow. Try to highlight the reasons you think justify such similarities in your case.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: What sort of reporting is acceptable if several students practice in the same organization?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: Every practioner will have a separate report as a rule. General outlook at the firm can be common for IE 400 only. However, you should choose separate examples each for reporting on your observations.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: If I am planning to work on a project full-time at the summer practice organization, is it possible for me to present the project work, instead of performing a practice according to the guidelines and submitting its results?

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: IE 400 practice may involve a project type study in which students have to supply a project report as explained in "IE 400 Summer Practice Manual" instead of defining an IE problem. Minimum duration for this type of IE 400 practice is 30 workdays (6 weeks). The project may be initiated long before you started your summer practice, or may be offered specifically to you by the organization, or you deem it as a potential area worth studying there. You may also consider getting fully involved in an ongoing project during your practice and desire to report on that only in your report.

title: FAQ |  Industrial Engineering Summer Practice
text: These students need to submit a two-pages project proposal. The proposal should include brief description of the company and details of the proposed project and an outline of what you will include in the report. Note that proposal should be approved (signed) by the company and be submitted to the summer practice committee by the first week of the summer practice. The committee shall evaluate the validity of your proposed work as a substitute for IE 400 summer practice. If it fulfills the requirements of the summer practice with the necessary observations you are expected to make, then you can submit a specially qualified report. The committee may ask you to add some parts from the regular content of the guidelines as well. However, in any case your report should be complete, in that you should describe all the phases of the work done including the issue, the organizational environment, the data or the facts collected, all the tools used, the outcomes of the project and its implementation.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 2. ANALYSIS OF THE MACRO ASPECTS

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 2.1 Production system is the heart of every organization as it consists of all activities

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: that add value to its output. A production system uses many inputs (e.g. materials,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: equipment, supplies, labor, energy, money, knowledge) some of which are the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: products of other organizations and transforms them into goods/ services. These

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: goods/ services may also be used as inputs to other production systems. Besides, a

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: production system interacts with its environment (e.g. customers, competitors,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: national economy, government, creditors, suppliers) during its operation.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Identify major items of input of the production system you have observed.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Specify where and how they are supplied (e.g., sources, means of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: transportation, volume and frequency of deliveries, usage rates etc.).

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 2.2 Any manufacturing organization performs its activities in some physical

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: environment consisting of land, buildings, warehouses, roads, shops, garages, docks,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: storages, etc. These are part of the facilities of the organization. In some cases not all

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: facilities of a firm are located on the same property and they may be far away from

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: each other, even in different cities.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Identify the major facilities of the manufacturing firm you observed during

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: your summer practice on a rough (free hand) sketch. Show a few items that

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: flow among them (e.g., painted parts, sheet metal, vehicles to repair, spare

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: parts, steam, fabric, design information, cardboard boxes, etc.).

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 2.3 When deciding on the location of a manufacturing facility, there are many factors to

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: be considered. Some of these are:

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: a) distribution needs for the products,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: b) availability or physical characteristics of raw materials,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: c) physical characteristics of the products,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: d) labor availability and quality,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: h) laws, taxation, incentives, government politics etc.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Specify the most prevailing factor for selecting the current location of the facility with regard

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: to the factors listed above or the like. Support your ideas. (You may use a sketch, a table, a

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: graph or a map, if necessary).

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 3. MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SYSTEM

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 3.1 Every organization has an information system which is designed to meet its

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: information requirements. In this system data are recorded, classified, summarized

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: and processed to produce information. Management information system should

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: support decision making at three different levels:

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: a) Strategic level decisions (e.g. plant expansion, determination of product lines,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: mergers, diversification, capital expenditures, etc.).

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: b) Tactical level - implementation of plans (e.g. allocation of resources to different

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: products, formulation of budgets, funds flow analysis, plant layout decisions,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: c) Operational level, day-to-day routine operations (e.g. receiving and shipping

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: operations, scheduling, inventory control, quality control and allocating workers

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Specify the decision makers (individual or group, their positions within the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: organizational structure) and the related subject of decision-making with

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: regard to one decision-making activity in each of these decision levels.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 3.2 Computers are widely used in processing data and providing information for

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: managerial decision making. They are also employed in organizations to improve

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: productivity and provide better utilization of resources. The physical units making

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: up a computer system are called hardware.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Identify the computer systems (computer networks, stand-alone PC’s,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: workstations, main frames etc. -their types and approximate capacities) in

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: use and their spread (functions or departments with extensive or low

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: computer support in their operations) in your practice organization.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4. AN OVERVIEW OF THE PRODUCTION SYSTEM

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.1 A production system takes inputs and transforms them into outputs with some

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: inherent value. The transformation process is, in fact, a flow process of input

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: materials and information. Material flows through several processes: It first flows

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: from supplier to the production system to become raw material inventory. It then

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: moves to the production floor, where the material conversion process takes place;

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: the material, in the form of work-in-process inventory (WIP), moves through

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: different workstations by traversing certain routes on the production floor. Finally,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: it becomes a finished product and stored in finished goods inventory.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Provide a schematic representation of the material flow of a particular

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: product in your practice organization. Note that your diagram should

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: include the complete flow from raw materials inventory through finished

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: goods inventory with every point of conversion (workstations, stock points)

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.2 Manufacturing processes can be categorized as follows:

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Those processes that are characterized by continuous flow as in steel making, sugar

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: refining and chemical processing are called continuous processes.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: When items are produced in large lots following an unchanging sequence of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: operations, the process becomes a repetitive process. Standardized product types

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: characterize it. Due to unchanging routing of parts, facilities can be arranged as a

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: flow shop. The automobile industry is a good example of a flow shop.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Intermittent processes are those processes in which items are processed in small lots

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: to customer specifications. Job shop, batch shop and project shop typify these. A job

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: shop produces low-volume highly customized products. Product routing varies

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: widely and facilities are arranged on a functional basis. Metal, plastic and

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: woodworking industries where non-standard products are processed are examples of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: job shops. Between the extremes of job shops and flows shops is the batch shop. In

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: batch shops, product variety is lower; batch sizes are large; and repetitiveness of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: operations is higher compared to job shops. Project shop produces a single,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: customized product such as large turbines, aircraft and ships.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: A manufacturing system may be a combination of the above classes.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Explain the type of operations in your practice organization with regards to

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: any one of the followings: production volume or product variety.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Describe your reasons in detail.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.3 In a production system, the material conversion process takes place on the production

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: floor, which is arranged in a certain way to facilitate conversion. Production volume

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: and product variety determine the type of arrangement or layout.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: One typical job shop layout is process layout in which all similar equipment and

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: operations are grouped together in the same department. For example, all stamping

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: is done in the press department. A flow shop, on the other hand, uses a product

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: layout. Equipment is arranged so that the product always follows the same routing

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: through the layout. For example, assembly line is a typical example for product

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: layout (automobile industry, home appliances, and electronics industry). Group

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: technology (GT) or cellular layout can be used to develop a hybrid between pure

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: process layout and pure product layout. The equipment is arranged into cells, each

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: containing the equipment used to process a particular family of parts. A project shop

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: uses a fixed-position layout. The product (aircraft, ship) stays in one place while the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: material and equipment are brought to it. Most plants are laid out using a

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Discuss the type or combinations of the types of layout you have observed in

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: your practice organization. Support your points using rough sketches.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.4 The flow and movement of materials and components within the plant is essential for

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: carrying out successive operations. This is referred to as materials handling.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Identify some of the materials handling equipment in the plant and state

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: where and for what purposes they are used. On a rough free-hand drawing,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: identify a path followed by any one of the materials handling equipment.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.5 Productivity implies the enhancement of the production process. Enhancement

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: means favorable comparison of the quantity of resources employed (inputs) to the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: quantity of goods and services produced (outputs). Productivity, then, is the ratio of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: the outputs produced for use outside of an organization, divided by the resources

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: used. It can be measured in a variety of ways, such as labor, capital, energy, material

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Compute / Describe an appropriate productivity measure for your practice

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.6 Based on the determination of standard times for each part/product, unit-

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: manufacturing costs can be estimated. Unit-manufacturing cost of a product has to

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: be determined to be utilized in various planning and decision making functions.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: There are three basic cost elements: direct material cost, direct labor cost and factory

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: overhead cost. Unit-manufacturing cost can be calculated as:

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Unit-manufacturing cost = Unit direct labor cost + Unit direct material cost +

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: allocated factory overhead to a unit.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Are unit-manufacturing costs calculated in your practice organization? If

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: yes, explain how they are calculated and provide an example. If no, describe

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: how expenses will be accounted for under different cost items for any one of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 4.7 Balance sheets and income statements are the basic tools to analyze the firm's

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: financial situation. Ratio analysis is often carried out for this purpose.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Carry out comparative ratio analysis using the balance sheets and income

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: statements for the last two years and evaluate the financial standing of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: the organization. (Calculate all the necessary ratios for such analysis), or

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: itemize titles for the balance sheet/income statement for the organization.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 5. PRODUCTION PLANNING AND CONTROL SYSTEM

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 5.1 Production planning and control is concerned with providing information to: (a)

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: efficiently manage the flow of materials, (b) effectively utilize people and equipment,

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: (c) coordinate internal activities with those of suppliers, and (d) communicate with

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: customers to meet their requirements. Production planning and control can be

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: viewed as a system. Its components (like managing the demand, supplying the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: materials, planning the deliveries, adjusting the capacity, etc.) contribute to the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: overall objectives of the organization through the cost, volume, quality and timeliness

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: Management of the types of products (so called product-mix) and their respective

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: quantities brings the problem of determining the demand. This may require analysis

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: of past data, collecting and processing of separate customer orders, signing contracts

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: for supply on an agreed-upon routine basis or conducting a market research

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: (especially for a new product).

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: State subjects of typical decisions on the types and quantities related to some

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: specific products of your practice organization. Who make(s) these

title: Ie300 Manual 1

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: organization? What is the basis for these decisions?

text: 5.2 When and how to produce is the subject in another set of decision making of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: production planning and control. This set of information conveys the decisions

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: related with the allocation of scarce (limited) resources needed for production.

text: 5.3 Almost every business stocks goods to ensure smooth and efficient running of its

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: operations. Inventories of various uses may exist in a firm: (a) stocks accumulated

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: against seasonal fluctuations, (b) stocks caused by receiving in large quantities, (c)

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: stocks of parts being processed due to movement in batches or processing rate

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: differences between successive stages, (d) stocks due to transport delays during

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: delivery. Hence inventory exists whenever it is necessary (or sometimes unavoidable)

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: to stock for the requirements over a specified time into the future. Decisions

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: regarding how much and when to order are typical in any production planning and

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: control system as problems in inventory management. Stocking large quantities

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: would require higher invested capital but would result in less frequent shortages and

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: placement of orders. On the other hand, little or no stocks would decrease the

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: invested capital, but would increase the frequency of ordering as well as the risk of

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: not satisfying requirements on time. Both extremes are costly.

text: 6. QUALITY PLANNING AND CONTROL SYSTEM

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: 6.1 There is little agreement on what constitutes quality. Most people conceive quality as

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: an attribute of a product or service that can be improved. However, quality is not

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: only associated with products and services, but also includes processes, environment

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: and people. It is an ever-changing state; what is considered quality today may not be

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: enough to be considered quality tomorrow. Hence, quality can be defined as a

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: dynamic state associated with products, services, processes, environments and

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: people, that meets or exceeds expectations.

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text: The following is just a few other definitions proposed for “quality”:

title: Ie300 Manual 1
text:  Quality is conformance to requirements.

text: 3. AN OVERVIEW OF THE PRODUCTION SYSTEM

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: 3.1 A production system takes inputs and transforms them into outputs with some

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: inherent value. The transformation process is, in fact, a flow process of input

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: materials and information. Production systems can be categorized into two classes

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: as manufacturing and service. In manufacturing, the inputs and outputs are

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: usually tangible, and the transformations are often physical. On the other hand,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: service-oriented production systems may have intangible inputs/outputs, such as

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: information, and transformations that may not be physical.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: 3.2 Capacity is the maximum output of a system in a given period. Capacity is normally

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: expressed as a rate, such as the number of tons of steel that can be produced per week,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: per month, or per year. For many companies, measuring capacity can be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: straightforward. It is the maximum number of units that can be produced in a

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: specific time period, for example, the number of cars assembled per month in the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: automobile industry. However, for some organizations, determining capacity can be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: more difficult. In job shop production systems, for example, the products are so

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: varied that defining capacity in terms of output is not meaningful. In such systems,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: capacity should be expressed in terms of resource inputs such as total work time

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: available, beds available/day in a hospital, or as a capacity vector indicating

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: production levels of products.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: The designed capacity (theoretical capacity) of a system is the maximum capacity

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: that can be achieved under ideal conditions. Most organizations operate their

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: facilities at a rate less than the designed capacity. They do so because they have

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: found that they can operate more efficiently when their resources are not stretched to

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the limit. This concept is called effective capacity or utilization. Utilization is the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: maximum capacity a firm can expect to achieve given its product mix, scheduling

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: method, maintenance program, and standards of quality. Another consideration is

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: efficiency.. Depending on how facilities are used and managed, it may be difficult to

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: reach 100% efficiency. Typically, efficiency is expressed as a percentage of the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: effective capacity. Then the rated capacity is a measure of the maximum useable

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: capacity of a particular facility. Rated capacity can be computed as:

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: Rated capacity = (Designed capacity) (Utilization) (Efficiency).

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: Those processes in manufacturing that are characterized by continuous flow as in

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: systems, the process becomes a repetitive process. Standardized product types

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: characterize it. Due to unchanging routing of parts, facilities can be arranged as a

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: flow shop. An automobile assembly line in manufacturing, cafeteria and university

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: registration as service systems are good examples of a flow shop.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: A job shop produces low-volume highly customized products. Product routing

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: varies widely and facilities are arranged on a functional basis. Metal, plastic,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: woodworking industries, and providing special-delivery mail service and service

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: department for an automobile dealership where non-standard products are processed,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: are examples of job shops. Between the extremes of job shops and flows shops is the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: batch shop.. In batch shops, product variety is lower; batch sizes are larger; and

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: repetitiveness of operations is higher compared to job shops. An example of a batch

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: manufacturer might be a company making small hand tools like drills of different

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: sizes; and examples of batch service might be catering, health care, and providing

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: standard service in groups like scheduling air or bus travel. Project shop produces a

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: single, customized product like large turbines, aircrafts, and ships in manufacturing

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: organizations, and developing software, management, consulting work, preparing for

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: a banquet in service organizations.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: A production system’s operation can also be classified as make-to-stock (MTS),

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: make-to-order (MTO), or assemble-to-order (ATO). This classification is based on

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the degree of interaction between the firm’s production function and the customers of

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the firm, with MTS involving the least amount of interaction and MTO the highest

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: degree of contact. The MTS firm produces in batches and carries finished-products

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: inventories, where products can be delivered from stocks. The small-appliance

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: industry, in which manufacturers build inventories for future sales, is an example.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: Since services cannot be stored, service firms cannot operate as an MTS system. In

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: MTO firms, no finished-products inventory is held, and customer orders are

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: backlogged; products are designed and produced under close collaboration between

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the firm and customer, only after the order is received. Jet engine manufacturing is

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: an example of MTO manufacturing, while an automobile repair shop is an MTO

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: service. ATO is a hybrid firm where parts and subassemblies are made according to

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: response to a dealer's order, provides an automatic or manual transmission, air

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: conditioner, interior options, etc.; and an example of an ATO service firm is a fast-

text: One typical job shop layout is process layout in which all similar equipment and

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: supervision and access by customers; outpatient clinics; travel agencies; insurance

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: companies. A flow shop, on the other hand, uses a product layout. Equipment is

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: arranged so that the product always follows the same routing through the layout.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: industry, home appliances, and electronics industry). Some services also may be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

text: INDUSTRIAL ENGINEERING PROBLEMS

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: You are required to identify, define and formulate an industrial engineering

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: You are advised to take the view outlined below (an excerpt from “Notes on

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: System Design” by Prof. Dr. Çağlar Güven, February 1998) in identifying and

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: Engineers are expected to ‘solve problems’.. To see what this means we can adopt a simplified

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: view: a problem is something that needs a solution but does not have one. At first sight the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: difficulty seems to be finding a solution but as far as IEs are concerned, often that’s not even half

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the difficulty. Forget about well-defined textbook problems and solutions. Real-life problems have

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: a bothersome habit: they don’t come singly. They stick firmly together and often we cannot tell one

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: from the other. Instead we observe a tangled web, and as we do so, we have to try hard to catch

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: glimpses of individual problems. The usual inclination is to forget about the other problems in the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: web once we believe we have identified one. We shall say more of this later; for the moment let me

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: put it like this: it may very well be better to spend more of your time trying to identify and

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: structure issues than trying to solve problems. In any given problem situation there will always be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: more than one issue involved. Consider for example, the design of a fast-food outlet: Forecasting

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the demand for food ingredients, scheduling the staff, pricing the foods, capacity planning,

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: planning daily purchases, selecting a location, training the staff and several other aspects similar to

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: these are the issues you have to consider. Which ones are you going to address? Structuring an

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: issue means studying and selecting one for further analysis using models within a systemic

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: framework. The reason why structuring issues is at least as important as solving problems can be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: explained as follows: We do not really know what we mean by a solution. When we talk about a

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: problem we imply that there exists a set of conditions that is less than satisfactory and needs

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: improvement. The nature of the improvement however is often not clear at all and the dynamics of

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the improvement process is equally complicated. The end result is obtained one way or another

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: and is likely to be the product of the joint effort of many people. One might say then that

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: suggesting questions can be more important, potentially more originative, than suggesting

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: answers. In this way issues will be unfolded that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. It all

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: comes to this: an IE will perhaps be most useful if she can point out meaningful problem areas and

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: if she can structure them; the rest will be collectively taken care of by the organization, one way or

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: another. But even so, this does not mean that you can forget about looking for solutions altogether;

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: for you see, looking for solutions is in fact part of looking for problems.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: Various industrial engineering problems exist in a production environment as

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: interwoven with each other. Deficiencies occurring in production planning may be

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: the consequence of ill-structured forecasting done by the marketing department.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: The problems encountered, say in raw material inventory holding, may be the

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: result of economic crisis experienced in the sectors providing the raw material.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: The low utilization of machinery may be due to high level of absenteeism among

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: workers for which the major reason could be poor industrial relations. Deficiencies

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: in production planning, problems in raw material inventory holding, and low

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1
text: utilization of machinery are all symptoms of the problems.

title: Ie400 Manufacturing Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: 2.1 A productive system is the heart of every organization. It consists of all the activities

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: that add value in the conversion of inputs to outputs. A productive system uses

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: many types of resources (e.g. materials, equipment, supplies, labor, energy, money,

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: information) some of which are the products of other organizations and transforms

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: them into goods or services as outputs. Service systems are regarded as intangible

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: output conversion systems while manufacturing systems are tangible output

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: conversion systems. However, there are cases where the productive system is a

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: combination of both. For example a retail store is generally considered to be a service

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: system, but its output consists of tangible items sold and the intangible utility of

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: offering an assortment of items in one location. In many services, the form of the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: resource does not change during the conversion process. For example real estate

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: services usually accept property as the owner supplies it to sell.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: In contrast to manufacturing, in service system one must distinguish “resources”

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: and “inputs”. For services, inputs are the customers, which arrive with unique

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: demands on service system, while resources are facilitating goods, labor, capital, etc.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: A service system must interact with the customers in order to function. In a self-

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: service system a customer is regarded beyond an input, as a co-producer. The

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: characteristics of the output also differ in a service system. Outputs may fall into one

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: of the three categories: (i) consumed simultaneously with its production (e.g. hair

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: cutting, medical treatment), (ii) in the form of information or energy packaged in a

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: storage device to be used later (e.g. book), and (iii) a supporting activity (e..g, interior

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: The outputs of one productive system may be used as resources to other productive

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: systems. Besides, a productive system interacts with its environment (e.g.,

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Services with low degree of labor-intensity and low degree of customization are

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: named service factories (airlines, hotels), services with low labor intensity but high

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: customization are named service shops. The analog of service shop in a

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: manufacturing system is job shop, and an example for service shop is auto-repair.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Services with high labor intensity and low customization are named mass services.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: The analog in a manufacturing system is flowshop, and examples are retailing,

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: education, cafeteria, university registration. Services with high labor intensity and

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: high customization are called professional services. The analog in a manufacturing

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: environment is project shop and examples are consultancy (e.g. lawyers, architects),

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: software development, or preparing for a banquet.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Services might be continuously delivered (police or fire protection, insurance) or

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: discretely transacted (mail service, movie theater). The analog in a manufacturing

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: system is continuous processes (such as steel, cement, sugar) versus discrete-part or

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: assembly manufacturing (such as automotive).

text: require any customer contact (auto-repair), or that are standardized but require

text: 3.4 The types of layouts in a service system can be as follows:

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: In fixed-position layout, the customer or item stays in one place while the material

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: and equipment are brought to that place. Examples are a house to be decorated, a roof

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: to be repaired, or a surgery operation. Sometimes the nature of the equipment does

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: not allow for mobility, for example heavy, expensive hospital equipment for kidney

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: dialysis requires the patients to a fixed location. Another type of layout is process

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: layout where the equipment with similar functionality are grouped at one place.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Examples are hospitals, beauty parlors. Retail stores group all similar products such

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: as hardware, sporting goods, and photographic equipment in separate departments

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: for ease of supervision and access by customer. In a product layout the number of

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: services provided is limited. The services are sequenced so that a smooth flow of the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: customers through the stations is maintained, and bottlenecks can be avoided by

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: balancing the time required to receive each piece of service. An example is the student

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: cafeteria where several food stations and a cashier form the sequence of services.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Fixed-position layout, process and product layouts exist in manufacturing systems

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: as well. Several other layout types that are specific to service systems are office

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

text: 5.1 There is little agreement on what constitutes quality. Most people conceive quality as

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: an attribute of a product or service that can be improved. However, quality is not

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: only associated with products and services, but also includes processes, environment

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: and people. Quality can be defined as a dynamic state associated with products,

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: services, processes, environments and people, that meets or exceeds expectations.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: According to research (Parasuraman et.al, 1985), the consumers assess the quality of

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: a service based on characteristics such as reliability, responsiveness, competence,

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: empathy and tangibles. Reliability involves consistency and dependability of a service

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: (for example in a restaurant the billing must be accurate). Responsiveness concerns

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: the timeliness of the service. Competence is about the knowledgeability and skill of the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: personnel that provides service. Empathy includes attributes such as approachability

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: of the personnel and how concerned the personnel is about the problems of the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: customers. Tangibles are related with the physical environment, such as the facilities

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: or appearance of the personnel.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Measuring the quality of a service is not easy due to the dominance of intangible (and

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: psychological) factors. The customers have an expected level of service. Even if a

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: company is able to perfectly identify the “expected service”, in the process of service

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: delivery discrepancies may occur, which may result in a gap between the perceived

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: service and the expected service. This gap may also occur due to company’s

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: (mis)perception of the customer expectations, not being able to translate the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: perceptions into quality specifications, or not being able to communicate the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: specifications well. For example, if a company creates an image that increases the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: customer expectations, quality ratings would be low even if the company meets the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: internal quality specifications.

text: 1. Identification and Definition of the Problem

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: Various industrial engineering problems exist in a production environment as

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: interwoven with each other. Deficiencies occurring in production planning may be

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: the consequence of ill-structured forecasting done by the marketing department.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: The problems encountered, say in raw material inventory holding, may be the

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: result of economic crisis experienced in the sectors providing the raw material.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: The low utilization of machinery may be due to high level of absenteeism among

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: workers for which the major reason could be poor industrial relations. Deficiencies

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: in production planning, problems in raw material inventory holding, and low

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: utilization of machinery are all symptoms of the problems.

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1
text: industrial engineering problem. Possible causes of the symptoms should be

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Ie400 Service Manual 1

title: Staj Protokolu
text: Lisans öğrencilerimiz için çeşitli kurumlarda kazanacakları deneyim, kuramsal bilgilerinin pekişmesi, değişik kurumlarda yapılan uygulamaları tanımaları ve çeşitli meslek gruplarının bir ekip olarak nasıl bir arada çalıştıklarını gözleyebilmeleri açısından çok önemlidir. Stajın amacı, Orta Doğu Teknik Üniversitesi öğrencilerinin ilgili kurumlarda, kuramsal eğitimlerinde öğrendikleri konuları bir danışmanın gözetimi altında gözlem ve uygulama yaparak pekiştirmeleridir. Staj dersinde öğrencilerden devam edecekleri kurum yetkililerince uygun görüldüğü takdirde, aşağıda belirtilen konularda deneyim kazanmaları beklenmektedir.

title: Staj Protokolu
text: 1. Gözlem Yapmak: Kurumun çeşitli faaliyetlerini ve kurumun işleyiş kurallarını 	izlemek.

title: Staj Protokolu
text: 2. Aktif Katılım ve Uygulama Yapmak: Kurum faaliyetlerine mümkün 	olduğunca aktif olarak katılmak ve alanındaki bilgi ve becerilerini kullanmak.

title: Staj Protokolu
text: Yukarıda belirtilen amaçlar doğrultusunda, lisans öğrencilerimizin, tam zamanlı olarak stajlarına devam etmeleri gerekmektedir. Öğrencilerin devamları, Bölüm tarafından yollanacak Staj Devam Formu  ile gittikleri kurum tarafından takip edilecektir.  Ayrıca, staj süresince öğrencinin gösterdiği performansın, Stajyer Performans Değerlendirme Formu kullanılarak kurum yetkilisi tarafından değerlendirilmesi istenecektir. Staj yapan öğrencilerin staj dönemi sonunda, staj yapılan kurum, faaliyetleri ve stajın kendilerine katkıları konularını içeren kapsamlı bir Staj Raporu hazırlamaları gerekmektedir.

title: Staj Protokolu
text: Öğrencinin stajdaki performansı; stajın yapıldığı kurumda öğrenciye danışmanlık yapan kişi tarafından doldurulan Staj Devam Formu ve Stajyer Performans Değerlendirme Formu ve de öğrencinin hazırlayacağı Staj Raporu dikkate alınarak, Bölümü’ndeki staj danışmanı olan öğretim üyesi tarafından değerlendirilir.

title: Staj Protokolu
text: Staj Devam Formu ve Stajyer Performans Değerlendirme Formu, bu protokolün imzalanmasından sonra staj yapacak öğrenci aracılığıyla ilgili kuruma gönderilir.
